title: Is a paid job seva?
hookLine: doing your job well is a way of serving
carry: seva is service with no reward in mind
tomorrow: a kid at the stall asks: why the plain steel bracelet?

lines: JASLEEN: NOT IF THEY PAY YOU.
cards: A photo of an apron and a crate of peaches, captioned: today's seva, six hours at the stall. The first comment is a heart from Maya. The second is from Jasleen: um, it's not seva if they pay you.
Simran types a reply. Deletes it. Types it again.
Jasleen isn't being mean. She just takes the word seriously. And so does Simran.

teach.b: Let both views speak. Jasleen's first. Seva is selfless service, given freely: at the gurdwara, in the langar, for anyone in need.
In the Sukhmani Sahib, on ang 286, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: the one who serves without wanting a reward reaches the Lord. Call a paid shift seva, and the word loses its edge.
Her best case: keep seva clear of wages, so you can always tell the two apart. Now Simran's.

teach.h: SIMRAN: A JOB DONE WITH CARE SERVES.
teach.b: Kirat, honest work, is itself part of the Sikh life, and the way you bring yourself to it, care, honesty, no shortcuts, can be the same way you bring yourself to the langar.
Her best case: if service only happens on Sundays, the other six days are spent on something less.
Look closely and they agree on more than the comments suggest.
Neither thinks a paycheck makes work holy. Neither thinks a cashier can't serve the person in front of her. The real line is the one in Guru Arjan's verse: without wanting a reward.
A wage is fine. Working only for the wage is the thing both are wary of. So Simran edits the caption: six hours at the stall, did the job as well as i could.
And she keeps the word seva for her Sunday langar shift, where nobody pays anyone.

how: Sikhs do seva freely at the gurdwara and in the langar; some also speak of doing their paid work with the same care, while others keep the word seva for unpaid service.

o: doing your job well as a way of serving others
working for free at your parents' business
taking a job at the gurdwara instead of a shop

games.q: two views of seva — tap the pairs.
p: a job done with care serves too

s: in Guru Arjan's verse, seva is service without wanting a reward
ang 286: the one who serves without wanting a reward reaches the Lord.
Sikhs agree that a paycheck makes any job seva
neither view thinks a paycheck makes work holy; some keep seva for unpaid service.
seva can only happen in the langar
some Sikhs see a job done well as service too; others keep the word for freely given work.

games.q: your coworker says calling a paid job 'seva' cheapens the word. what's the best case for her view?
o: keeping seva clear of wages keeps 'without wanting a reward' plain to see.
she probably just doesn't like her own job very much.
paid work can't ever be honest, so it can't be service.
games.why: that's Jasleen's view at its strongest, straight from ang 286. Simran's view has a strong case too; they agree more than they differ.

practice: Choose one small task within reach, folding a towel, wiping a surface, straightening a shelf, and do it as well as you possibly can, slowly, corners and all. Then sit with the finished thing in view.

wordCard.voice: Work as seva. Doing your job well as a way of serving, without making the reward the reason.

carryVoice: Your line: seva is service with no reward in mind. The wage is fine; it just isn't the reason. Done for today.

sources.ref: Ang 286 (Gauri Sukhmani, Guru Ashtapadi 18, Guru Arjan: sevaa karat hoe nihkaamee, tis kau hot paraapat suaamee), paraphrased
